lessons.title: Designing Outdoor Pens and Enclosures
lessons.body: Outdoor snail pens are the cheapest way to start, but they must be built right or you will lose snails to predators and escape. Choose a site with loose, moist soil rich in organic matter, partial shade (like under banana or pawpaw trees), and a gentle slope so water never pools. Avoid low-lying areas that flood. In West Africa, many farmers use a pen size of 2 meters by 3 meters for 500 to 1,000 adult snails. Build the pen walls with concrete blocks, treated wood, or mud bricks, sunk 20 cm into the ground to stop burrowing predators. The wall should be 50â60 cm high. Leave a 10 cm overhang at the top, angled inward, to prevent snails from climbing out. Inside, add a 5â10 cm layer of loose topsoil mixed with compost. Plant leafy vegetables like cocoyam, sweet potato, or lettuce as both food and ground cover. Provide flat stones, broken pots, or palm fronds as shelters where snails hide during the day. A simple water dish (shallow, 2 cm deep) helps maintain humidity. For rain protection, cover the pen with a shade net or palm fronds on a simple bamboo frame. In dry season, mist the pen twice daily. Clean the pen every two weeks, removing leftover food and checking for small holes. A well-designed outdoor pen can produce 200â300 snails per square meter per cycle. Remember, snails are escape artistsâany gap wider than 2 cm is an exit. Use fine mesh (1 mm) over drainage holes. In East Africa, farmers often use raised wooden boxes (1 m x 2 m) with mesh bottoms for better drainage. Always test your pen with a few snails for a week before introducing your main stock.

lessons.title: Constructing Indoor Climate-Controlled Units
lessons.body: Indoor snail units give you year-round production, especially in dry or cold regions. You can convert a spare room, garage, or build a simple shed. The key is controlling temperature (22â28Â°C), humidity (75â90%), and ventilation. Start with a room of at least 3 m x 4 m. Insulate the walls and ceiling with polystyrene or mud-straw mix if you are in a hot area. For cooling, use a cheap evaporative cooler (a fan blowing over wet sacks) or an air conditioner if you have power. For heating in cold highlands, use a small greenhouse heater or a wood stove with a chimney, but never let smoke enter the snail area. Build shelves from treated wood or plastic, 1 m wide, with 40 cm between tiers. Each shelf holds plastic trays (60 cm x 40 cm x 15 cm) with lids. Drill 5 mm ventilation holes along the sides and cover them with fine mesh. Inside each tray, put 3 cm of moist coco peat or sterilized soil. Keep a shallow water dish. Use a hygrometer (costs about $10) and a thermometer to monitor conditions. Mist the trays twice daily with a hand sprayer. A small fan on low speed circulates air but avoid direct drafts. For lighting, use a 40-watt bulb or LED on a 12-hour timer; snails are nocturnal but need a day-night cycle. Clean trays weekly, removing uneaten food and replacing soil monthly. A 3 m x 4 m room can hold 40 trays, producing about 2,000 snails per cycle. In Nigeria, farmers use old refrigerators with the compressor removed as mini climate chambers for breeding. Always ensure a backup water source for misting. This setup costs between $200 and $500, but pays back in one year.

lessons.title: Choosing Materials for Snail Housing
lessons.body: The materials you choose determine cost, durability, and snail health. Never use treated wood with toxic preservatives (like creosote or pentachlorophenol) because snails absorb chemicals through their skin. Instead, use untreated hardwood (e.g., iroko, mahogany), bamboo, or plastic. For outdoor pens, concrete blocks (15 cm x 20 cm x 40 cm) are bestâthey last 10+ years and stop predators. A 2 m x 3 m pen needs about 50 blocks, costing $30â$50. Mud bricks are cheaper but dissolve in heavy rain; use them only in dry areas and reinforce with cement plaster. For indoor trays, food-grade plastic is ideal. You can buy new trays ($3â$5 each) or repurpose used ones from bakeries. Avoid metal trays because they rust and can leach zinc, which is toxic to snails. For mesh, use plastic mosquito netting (1 mm holes) or aluminum screen. Metal chicken wire (1 cm holes) is okay for large pens but small snails can escape. For bedding, coco peat (coir) is excellentâit holds moisture, resists mold, and costs about $5 for a 5 kg block that expands to 50 liters. Sterilize soil by baking it in an oven at 120Â°C for 30 minutes or pouring boiling water over it. For shelters, use broken clay pots, roof tiles, or palm fronds. For water dishes, use shallow plastic lids or ceramic saucers. For climbing, add small branches or PVC pipes. In Kenya, farmers use old tires cut in half as cheap shelters. For shade, use shade net (70% shade) or woven palm mats. Always check that materials are non-toxic: if it smells like chemicals, don't use it. Buy from local hardware stores or agricultural suppliers. A complete 2 m x 3 m outdoor pen with concrete blocks, mesh, and bedding costs about $80â$120. Indoor trays cost $2â$4 per snail capacity of 50 snails. Choose materials that are easy to clean and replace.

lessons.title: Predator-Proofing Your Snail Farm
lessons.body: Predators can wipe out your snails in one night. The main enemies are ants, rats, mice, birds, lizards, snakes, frogs, millipedes, and beetles. Ants are the worstâthey eat eggs and young snails. To stop ants, create a moat around your pen: dig a 15 cm wide, 10 cm deep trench and fill it with water or used engine oil. Reapply oil monthly. Alternatively, place pen legs in containers of water. For rats and mice, use snap traps or poison bait stations outside the pen, never inside. Cover the pen with a tight lid or mesh (1 mm) at night. For birds, use shade net or bird netting over the top. For lizards and snakes, keep the area around the pen clear of tall grass and debris. Seal all cracks in walls with cement. For millipedes and beetles, handpick them daily and drop them in soapy water. For frogs, remove any standing water nearby. In West Africa, farmers use a mixture of wood ash and chili powder sprinkled around the pen baseâants and millipedes hate it. Reapply after rain. For indoor units, screen all windows and doors with fine mesh. Use sticky traps for crawling insects. Never use pesticides inside snail pensâthey will kill your snails. If you have a serious ant problem, use ant gel bait placed outside the pen. Check your pen every morning for signs of predators: disturbed soil, empty shells, or slime trails leading away. A well-protected pen can reduce losses from 50% to under 5%. In Uganda, a farmer lost 2,000 snails to ants in one night; after installing a water moat, losses stopped. Spend 10% of your budget on predator-proofingâit is the best investment.

lessons.title: Lighting, Ventilation, and Temperature Control
lessons.body: Snails are nocturnal and prefer dark, humid conditions, but they still need a natural day-night cycle for breeding. In outdoor pens, natural shade from trees provides the right light. If you use shade net, choose 70â80% shadeâtoo much light stresses snails, too little dries them out. For indoor units, use a 40-watt incandescent bulb or a 10-watt LED on a timer set for 12 hours on, 12 hours off. Place the light at least 1.5 m above trays to avoid heat spots. Avoid fluorescent tubes that emit UV; UV harms snails. Ventilation is critical to prevent mold and ammonia buildup. In outdoor pens, leave gaps at the top of walls (covered with mesh) for air flow. In indoor rooms, install a small exhaust fan (100 CFM) on one wall and an intake vent on the opposite wall. Run the fan for 10 minutes every hour. You can also use passive vents: 10 cm diameter PVC pipes with mesh caps, one low and one high. Temperature should stay between 22Â°C and 28Â°C. Above 30Â°C, snails become inactive and can die. Below 15Â°C, they stop growing. Use a thermometer (min-max type, $5) to monitor. For cooling, mist the floor and walls with water, or use a fan over a wet cloth. For heating in cold areas, use a small greenhouse heater or a 60-watt ceramic heat emitter (for a 1 mÂ³ area). Never place heaters directly in trays. Humidity should be 75â90%. Use a hygrometer ($10). If humidity drops below 70%, mist more often or add wet sponges. If it stays above 95%, increase ventilation to prevent mold. In the Sahel, farmers dig indoor pits 1 m deep to keep temperatures stable. In highlands, a simple polytunnel works. Always keep a backup power source for fans and heaters if you rely on electricity.

lessons.title: Cost-Effective Housing Solutions for Small-Scale Farms
lessons.body: You don't need a lot of money to house snails. Start with what you have. A used plastic basin (50 cm diameter) with a lid can hold 50 adult snails. Drill 10 small holes in the lid for air, add 3 cm of moist soil, and place it in a shaded spot. Cost: $2. For a larger setup, use old tires. Cut one sidewall out, stack two tires, fill with soil, and cover with mesh. Each tire stack holds 100 snails. Cost: free. Wooden crates from markets (60 cm x 40 cm x 30 cm) can be lined with plastic sheeting and mesh. Cost: $1â$2 each. For a 2 m x 3 m pen, use bamboo poles and mud. Dig holes for corner posts, weave bamboo for walls, and plaster with mud mixed with cow dung (which repels ants). Cover with palm fronds. Total cost: $10â$20. In East Africa, farmers use old jerrycans cut in halfâeach holds 20 snails. For indoor, use plastic shelves from a hardware store ($20) and stack plastic trays. A 1 m x 2 m shelf unit holds 10 trays, each with 50 snails, so 500 snails for $40. For climate control, use a wet burlap sack over a fanâcost $5. For heating, a 60-watt bulb in a metal tin works for a small cabinet. Always prioritize predator-proofing: a water moat around a tire stack costs nothing but saves snails. Collect rainwater in a barrel for misting. Make your own coco peat by soaking coir blocks. In Nigeria, a farmer built a 4 m x 4 m pen with mud bricks and bamboo for under $50 and produced 1,500 snails in 6 months. Start small, reinvest profits. A $100 budget can build a 2 m x 3 m concrete pen with mesh and bedding. Remember, snails multiply fastâ500 adults can become 5,000 in a year. So invest in quality where it matters: predator-proofing and moisture control. Cheap does not mean flimsy. Use free materials creatively, but never compromise on snail safety.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Snail Housing and Infrastructure

In African heliciculture, housing is not a cost centre â it is the production engine. A well-designed snail house controls the three variables that determine your gross margin: humidity (snails need 70â90% RH), temperature (optimal 20â28Â°C for Achatina achatina and A. fulica), and predator pressure (ants, rats, snakes, birds, millipedes and lizards can wipe out a cohort overnight). Get the infrastructure right and you can stock 60â120 snails per mÂ² of usable floor; get it wrong and mortality will exceed 40% before first harvest.

This reference lesson consolidates the six core lessons in this module into decision-ready guidance for small and medium-scale African snail farms â from a 20 mÂ² backyard pen in Kumasi to a 200 mÂ² semi-commercial unit in Ogun State or Nakuru.

1. Design Logic: Outdoor vs Indoor

Use outdoor pens where rainfall is 1,000â2,500 mm and shade trees are available; use indoor climate-controlled units where you need year-round production, disease isolation, or premium-market consistency. Many profitable African farms run a hybrid: outdoor pens for grow-out (cheaper per mÂ²) and a small indoor hatchery/nursery for eggs and juveniles (highest mortality stage).

2. Materials Selection Matrix

Material choice is the single biggest driver of build cost and lifespan. The table below uses 2024 indicative prices from West and East African suppliers; adjust to your local market.

Table 1: Snail Housing Material Options â Cost, Lifespan and Suitability
Material Typical cost (USD/mÂ²) Lifespan Best use Watch-outs
Wooden frame + wire mesh4â92â4 yrsBackyard pens, nurseriesTermites; treat timber
Concrete block + mesh lid18â3015+ yrsCommercial grow-outHigher capex; needs drainage
Bamboo + shade net2â51â2 yrsLow-cost starter pensRot, replacement cost
HDPE plastic trays/racks10â225â8 yrsIndoor climate unitsUV degradation outdoors

Sources: FAO, Snail Farming in West Africa: A Practical Guide (2008); AgriBiz Africa supplier surveys (2023â2024); NABARD, Snail Farming Handbook (India, adapted).

3. Stocking Density and Space Planning

Overcrowding is the most common cause of stunted growth in African snail farms. Plan your build around target stocking, not the other way round.

Table 2: Recommended Stocking Density by Life Stage
Life stage Snails per mÂ² Substrate depth Target RH Target temp.
Hatchlings (0â4 wks)200â3005â8 cm85â90%24â27Â°C
Juveniles (1â3 mo)80â12010â15 cm80â85%23â27Â°C
Grow-out (3â6 mo)40â6015â20 cm75â85%22â28Â°C
Breeders10â1520â25 cm80â90%24â28Â°C

Sources: Cobbinah, Vink & Onwuka, Snail Farming in West Africa (FAO/CTA, 2008); IFAD, Smallholder Livestock Diversification Brief (2021).

4. Predator-Proofing: The African Reality

In tropical Africa, predator losses typically account for 15â30% of stock in unprotected pens. The layered defence that works:

  • Perimeter moat: 10 cm sand or wood-ash ring around every pen â blocks ants, millipedes and slugs.
  • Mesh aperture â¤ 1 cm: stops rats, snakes, birds and lizards. Weld mesh, not chicken wire.
  • Raised legs: indoor racks on 30 cm legs sitting in oil cups â the classic ant defence.
  • Roof overhang: 30 cm overhang stops rain entry and deters climbing predators.
  • Regular inspection: ants colonise within 48 hours; walk the perimeter twice weekly.
â  SAFETY WARNING â Pesticide Use Around Snails

Never apply chemical insecticides, molluscicides, or rat poison inside or within 5 metres of snail pens. Snails absorb toxins through their skin and will die or accumulate residues that make them unsafe for human consumption and export. Use physical barriers, hand-collection, and â where absolutely necessary â food-grade diatomaceous earth at the perimeter only. Wear gloves and a mask when handling any treatment, and wash hands before entering pens. If you suspect contamination, quarantine the cohort and do not sell it.

5. Lighting, Ventilation and Temperature Control

Snails are nocturnal and photophobic â direct sunlight is lethal. In outdoor pens, use 60â70% shade netting and orient pens eastâwest so the long axis receives even light. In indoor units, use diffuse LED lighting on 12-hour cycles to stabilise breeding rhythms, and cross-ventilation with mesh vents on opposite walls. In the Sahel and northern Nigeria, evaporative cooling (wicking walls, wet sand floors) keeps indoor temperatures within 22â28Â°C during the hot season. In the humid forest belt, ventilation is about removing excess moisture to prevent fungal rot â not adding it.

6. Cost-Effective Housing for Small-Scale Farms

A profitable 20 mÂ² starter pen can be built for USD 180â350 using locally sourced bamboo, termite-treated timber, and shade netting. The three highest-return upgrades, in order:

  1. Mesh lid (predator loss reduction pays back in one season).
  2. Sand moat (cheapest ant control available).
  3. Shade netting (reduces heat mortality by 20â35%).

Avoid the temptation to build a large pen before you have proven your hatchery. Build small, prove 80%+ survival, then scale.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Site pen on well-drained ground, away from low-lying flood zones.
  • â Install 60â70% shade netting and orient pens eastâwest.
  • â Fit mesh lid with â¤ 1 cm aperture, hinged for daily access.
  • â Create a 10 cm sand or wood-ash moat around every pen perimeter.
  • â Use loamy substrate 15â20 cm deep, pH 6.5â7.5, mixed with crushed limestone or oyster shell.
  • â Provide a drainage trench on the downhill side of the pen.
  • â Mount a cheap hygrometer/thermometer inside each pen â record daily.
  • â Never store pesticides, fuel or rodenticide within 5 m of pens.
  • â Inspect perimeter for ant trails and rodent burrows twice weekly.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Small-Scale Snail Production and Marketing (Diversification Booklet)
  • IFAD â Smallholder Livestock Diversification Knowledge Brief
  • CABI Invasive Species Compendium â Achatina fulica (biosecurity & containment)
  • USDA National Agricultural Library â Snails and Heliciculture Resource List

quiz.q: What is the recommended height for an outdoor snail pen wall?
quiz.explanation: A 50â60 cm wall with an inward overhang prevents snails from climbing out.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid treated wood with creosote in snail housing?
options: C) It is toxic to snails
quiz.explanation: Snails absorb chemicals through their skin, and creosote is poisonous to them.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for indoor snail units?
quiz.explanation: Snails are most active and grow best between 22Â°C and 28Â°C.

quiz.q: Which material is best for indoor snail trays?
quiz.explanation: Food-grade plastic is non-toxic, easy to clean, and does not rust like metal.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a water moat around a snail pen?
quiz.explanation: A water moat is a barrier that prevents ants from reaching the snails.

quiz.q: How often should you mist an outdoor snail pen in dry season?
quiz.explanation: Misting twice daily maintains the high humidity snails need in dry conditions.

quiz.q: What is the recommended shade percentage for outdoor snail pens?
quiz.explanation: 70â80% shade net provides the dim, humid conditions snails prefer without overheating.

quiz.q: Which of these is a cheap predator-proofing method for small farms?
quiz.explanation: A water moat is nearly free and effectively stops ants and other crawling predators.

quiz.q: What is the best way to sterilize soil for snail bedding?
quiz.explanation: Baking soil at 120Â°C kills pathogens and pest eggs without toxic chemicals.

quiz.q: How many adult snails can a 2 m x 3 m outdoor pen hold?
quiz.explanation: A well-designed 2 m x 3 m pen can sustainably hold 500â1,000 adult snails.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using coco peat as bedding?
options: B) It holds moisture and resists mold
quiz.explanation: Coco peat retains water well and is naturally mold-resistant, ideal for humid snail habitats.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid metal trays for snails?
options: B) They rust and leach zinc
quiz.explanation: Rusting metal can release zinc, which is toxic to snails.

quiz.q: What is the recommended ventilation rate for an indoor snail room?
options: D) Once a day for 1 hour
quiz.explanation: Running a fan for 10 minutes every hour prevents mold and ammonia buildup without drying the room.

quiz.q: Which predator is the most destructive to snail eggs and young snails?
quiz.explanation: Ants can quickly kill and carry away eggs and hatchlings, causing heavy losses.

quiz.q: What is a cost-effective indoor heating method for a small snail cabinet?
options: B) 60-watt bulb in a metal tin
quiz.explanation: A 60-watt bulb in a metal tin provides gentle, localized heat at low cost.

quiz.q: How often should you clean an outdoor snail pen?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning every two weeks removes spoiled food and prevents pest buildup.

quiz.q: What is a good natural ant repellent for around snail pens?
options: B) Wood ash and chili powder
quiz.explanation: Wood ash and chili powder create a barrier ants avoid, and it is safe for snails.

quiz.q: What is the ideal humidity range for indoor snail units?
quiz.explanation: 75â90% humidity keeps snails moist and active without encouraging mold.

quiz.q: Which of these is a free material for building a small snail pen?
quiz.explanation: Old tires are often free and can be stacked and filled with soil to make a pen.

quiz.q: Why is it important to have a day-night light cycle for indoor snails?
options: C) To make them grow faster
quiz.explanation: A consistent light cycle helps regulate snails' reproductive behavior.

quiz.q: What is the best way to prevent snails from escaping through drainage holes?
quiz.explanation: Fine mesh allows water drainage but blocks even tiny snails from escaping.

quiz.q: What is a cheap alternative to a commercial hygrometer for checking humidity?
options: B) A wet cloth and fan
quiz.explanation: A hair hygrometer is a low-cost DIY option that indicates humidity changes.

quiz.q: How deep should you sink pen walls into the ground to stop burrowing predators?
quiz.explanation: Sinking walls 20 cm deep prevents rats, mice, and other burrowers from digging under.

quiz.q: What is a good shelter material for snails inside a pen?
quiz.explanation: Broken clay pots provide dark, moist hiding spots that snails naturally seek.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using pesticides inside snail pens?
quiz.explanation: Pesticides are toxic to snails and can wipe out your entire stock.

quiz.q: What is the recommended size of a plastic basin for holding 50 adult snails?
quiz.explanation: A 50 cm diameter basin with a lid provides enough space for 50 adult snails.

quiz.q: What is a cost-effective way to cool an indoor snail room in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: A fan blowing over wet sacks creates evaporative cooling at very low cost.

quiz.q: How often should you replace the soil in indoor snail trays?
quiz.explanation: Replacing soil monthly prevents waste buildup and disease.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of using a raised wooden box with mesh bottom for outdoor pens?
quiz.explanation: A mesh bottom allows excess water to drain, preventing waterlogging.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of predator activity in a snail pen?
options: B) Empty shells and slime trails
quiz.explanation: Empty shells and disturbed slime trails indicate that predators have been feeding.
